hits.name: Sprytix
hits.text:
ANTHROPIC LEAKED A FILE WHERE 4 AGENTS BUILD A BUSINESS DOING $100K A MONTH IN 60 MINUTES

four agents run around the clock, cost $0 and work against a $100,000 target

scout → architect → 2 builders → critic → back to root

what makes it a team isn't the four agents, it's the three contracts written between them

the scout hands the architect who already ships this and what they charge

the architect hands the builders a spec with the interfaces named

the builders hand the critic a diff and the tests that cover it

leave any one of those boundaries vague and the work goes missing exactly there

Haiku 4.5 triages cheap, Opus 5 decides expensive, Sonnet 5 builds, Opus 5 judges

the most expensive model runs twice: once to plan, once to pass verdict

two builders in parallel is two ways to disagree - which is exactly what the gate is for

$100,000 is 334 customers at $299, $50,000 is 167, $10,000 is 34

and what you pay isn't even visible on that same scale

the cost was never the thing standing in your way

save this and paste it into Claude Code - let it write your 3 contracts ↓

hits.name: Argona
hits.text:
i honestly don't get why people still let their AI forget them

the week GPT-6 Astra came out i gave it a folder and one rule: "write down everything you learn. reread it before every job"

the glass ball is that folder 19 days later. 165,000 leaves: 41,000 files, 118,000 calls, 6,000 notes to itself. one root, my first sentence

the idea is simple: you stop explaining yourself. it starts every job already knowing your lease, your bank and your printer, and gets faster every time

what Astra does with that folder:

→ reads it before it types a word. sorting my receipts: first time an hour, fourth time 6 minutes
→ asks a question and keeps working while it waits. ignore it, my mac beeps
→ runs a 2am routine on every note marked "later". a monitor port dead for a year got fixed on a saturday night, 4-minute flash
→ writes itself rules. after a subscription charged me twice: "check the bank export before anything renews". 14 mornings in a row since
→ hands boring reading to cheaper helpers, keeps the thinking. a full evening costs about 10% of my weekly limit

at first i thought the picture was a glitch. it's just 19 days of not forgetting

copy this today:

> open codex, pick GPT-6 Astra, effort on high. the $20 plan is enough
> make a folder called memory with a file called AGENTS.md. codex reads that file first, every time
> paste one line: "before every task read this folder. after every task write what you learned and what broke"
> drop in anything about your life: the lease, a bank export, the manual for the thing that never worked
> give it one job tonight and end with: "remember"
> tomorrow, ask it something you only ever said once

one folder and six lines. after that you never explain yourself twice

the catch: the folder gets fat and eats the weekly limit. every sunday it prunes dead branches, 20 minutes

the people doing this don't post about it. their Astra already knows their landlord and their bank. yours meets you as a stranger every morning

every chat you close tonight is a branch you'll never get back

my rules file, link below

bookmark this before you close another chat

hits.name: Argona
hits.text:
a girl lying in bed makes $12,380 a month posting 12-second ai cartoons for toddlers. her whole studio is a $21 tab called swagga and a macbook she never opens past the browser

the number she doesn't say on camera: every cartoon goes up on 6 channels in 6 countries, because a 12-second cartoon for a 2-year-old has no language to translate

same file. six paychecks

i watched the clip 4 times before i got what she's actually selling. the cartoon is not the product. the product is a toddler who doesn't care who made it

the whole job is copying. she opens youtube, finds a kids show with 41m views, scrolls to the description, and the transcript is sitting there for free

→ paste the transcript into swagga's chat tab, ask for a prompt for a show inspired by it, 30 seconds
→ copy that prompt into the video tab, model sora 2, 9:16, 12 seconds
→ one generation, one file, about 4 minutes of waiting
→ upload to youtube shorts, instagram reels and tiktok from the phone
→ then to 5 more youtube channels titled in spanish, portuguese, hindi, arabic and indonesian, same file, no edit
→ 5 cartoons a day, 8 uploads each, 40 uploads, 38 minutes of her morning

youtube's own rule makes volume the whole game: a channel enters the partner program at 1,000 subscribers and 10,000,000 shorts views in 90 days. a toddler channel posting 5 times a day got there, in her telling, on day 61

month one: 1 channel, 2 cartoons a day, $212
month three: 6 channels, still 2 a day, $2,940
month six: 6 channels, 5 a day, $12,380

tuesday 7:40 am, youtube studio on her phone: "your channel is now eligible for shorts ad revenue sharing" on the third country channel. she was still in bed

the catch is real. anything marked made for kids gets no personalized ads, contextual only, so one view is worth a fraction of a normal short. she's not beating that. she's posting the same 12 seconds 6 times

and sora won't draw the real characters, copyrighted ones get rejected, so the prompt gives the bunny a new name and a new color. the toddler doesn't notice

$21 a month for the tab. $12,380 back. she recorded the tutorial from the same bed

six channels, one cartoon, zero words

hits.name: Mr. Buzzoni
hits.text:
CLAUDE + OBSIDIAN + LOOP ENGINEERING = A VAULT THAT RUNS ITSELF

the core idea: the vault is the loop's state, not the chat window

everything Claude knows lives in a .md file

the loop:
> capture - a thought lands in 00-inbox
> context - Claude Opus 5 pulls links, tags, and neighbouring notes
> draft - edits happen inside a git worktree, never the live vault
> review - a critic agent checks the diff before anything ships
> commit - appended to the vault, nothing gets rewritten

the key insight: frontmatter fields like supports, contradicts, and supersedes are graph edges, not metadata - the note format is the write API

start with a plain loop, it runs about 2-4x the cost of one direct call

> only move to a full graph once state has to outlive the session, several agents need to coordinate, or you have to explain what changed - that jump can run 10-50x

one review assistant climbed from 55% to 72% to 84% just by moving through these shapes in order

worth stealing even without a graph: the review step. most vaults skip it - claude writes straight to live notes

errors compound silently for months

set that gate first
hits.hook: Claude + Obsidian + Loop Engineering = a vault that runs itself — the vault is the loop's state, frontmatter edges are the write API, and the review gate is the piece most vaults skip until errors compound for months.

hits.name: NO1ennn
hits.text:
this is f*cking beyond comprehension.

Google engineers just shipped the entire agent lifecycle in one release: build, scale, govern. and every piece answers a specific way agents die in production

> context layers (Static, Turn, User, Cache): you decide what the model carries between turns, so token spend stops being a mystery
> a self heal plugin: the agent notices a tool call failed and retries it a different way instead of dying mid run
> adk deploy: one command from your laptop to the managed runtime, no packaging, no infra ticket
> Go joins Python and Java, with its own A2A SDK

then the part nobody builds for themselves:

> a dashboard on token consumption, latency, error rates and tool calls: the four things that actually kill an agent
> a traces tab that opens the real sequence of actions the agent took, step by step
> a playground wired to the deployed agent, past sessions included, so debugging is not a redeploy loop
> an Evaluation Layer with a User Simulator, because you cannot unit test a non deterministic system

and the part that decides whether it ever ships:

> agents get native identities as first class IAM principals: least privilege applies to them like it does to people
> Model Armor screens prompt injection, tool calls and responses, inline for Gemini or over REST
> Security Command Center inventories every agentic asset and flags data exfiltration by an agent

ADK is already at 7 million downloads. the runtime has a free tier, and express mode runs off a Gmail address.

the prototype was never the hard part.

hits.text:
this paper from the university of tokyo is pure f*cking treasure

it introduces AI Economist Agent: a framework that lets agents analyse financial risk without making up the numbers

evidence → model → test → report

AI Economist Agent turns macro-financial analysis into a controlled loop:

evidence sources → economic channels → registered models → acceptance tests → report

the LLM plans the work, retrieves evidence and organizes mechanisms

the knowledge graph keeps every relation tied to a source, date and scope

the quantitative model produces the number

the test decides whether that number can enter the report

the clever part:

the framework applies test-driven development to analytical claims

you define the contract before the result exists:

source eligibility → connected path → compatible model → passed numerical test → released report

this is how you let agents work through new risk scenarios without turning a fluent narrative into fake analysis

you can also build anything with GPT-6 Astra
hits.hook: A University of Tokyo paper framed as pure treasure — the kind of academic drop that creators turn into a threadable flex: rare, dense, and instantly screenshot-able.
hits.draft_en:
TOKYO JUST DROPPED A PAPER THAT SHOULD MAKE EVERY AGENT BUILDER UNCOMFORTABLE

Not a demo. Not a vibe post. A research cut that treats memory, tools, and loops like engineering — the same stack X has been cosplaying for months.

> intake is not storage
> a gate decides what survives
> conflict does not overwrite history

Most agent setups still stuff the last N messages into the prompt and call it memory.
This paper is the receipt that that approach is a toy.

If your agent forgets the constraint that made the last run work, you do not have an agent.
You have a chat with amnesia.

Steal the framing. Wire one gate. Ship before the timeline invents a worse version of this.

Today I hooked its neural connectome directly into a synthesizer.

139,255 neurons. 54.5 million synapses. 10ms reaction time.

While humans spend decades learning music theory, a fly's brain is out here in real time composing complex piano variations on Opus 01 in E Minor.

My previous posts proved it can beat the stock market and demolish FPS lobbies. Today it is casually writing better neoclassic piano solos than most humans.

If a fly's connectome can play a piano recital at this level, what is your excuse?

hits.name: slash1s
hits.text:
The $1M AI business math gets weird when $10K buys you five shots instead of one.

The thing is fucking gold, and the shift is not that Kimi K3 magically turns $10K into $1M. 

It makes every build, test and failure dramatically cheaper.

$10K -> Idea 1 -> Fail -> Idea 2 -> Fail -> Idea 3 -> First paying users.

At $1,000 per month you need 84 customers to cross $1M ARR. At $250 you need 334. That is a distribution problem, not a coding problem.

The best targets are boring workflows companies already spend real money on: research, monitoring, support, reporting, compliance, sales prep.

A company burning $12,000 a month on three people watching competitors will pay $1,000 for a tool that halves it.

AI changes the economics of being wrong. The founder who can afford five serious attempts beats the one betting everything on attempt #1.

The full playbook, budget and math are in the article ↓

hits.name: Ridark
hits.text:
A Grok Bot team reportedly produced 214 verified prospects, 89 approved outreach drafts and 11 content pieces in its first week. The operating design behind it is public. 

The setup revolves around Atlas, a chief-of-staff bot. The founder gives it an outcome. Atlas breaks the work down, assigns it and brings back a morning plan and a nightly delivery summary.

The specialists have narrower jobs.

Scout qualifies prospects and passes the verified set to Pitch, which prepares an opening message and two follow-ups. Quill drafts content from the company's learnings. Vault sorts the inbox. Ledger identifies the next metric that deserves attention.

One design choice connects the whole team: each chat belongs to an outcome. Atlas is in every one. A handoff records what finished, what is blocked and what the next bot should do. That gives the founder a place to inspect progress without rebriefing every specialist.

The video makes the teaching step concrete. Around 8:18, the walkthrough moves into screen recording, with a real website used as a worked example. Later, it shows a recurring-run schedule. The role brief gets a demonstration of how the work should happen. 

Sending, publishing, spending and irreversible decisions stay behind owner approval.

Six starting roles are documented in the repository. The post mentions eight.. the repo says to add the final two once the team is stable. It also frames the week-one figures as scoreboard targets.

The sheet maps the published team, its handoffs, role contracts and the useful points in the video.
hits.hook: A Grok Bot team reportedly hit 214 verified prospects, 89 outreach drafts and 11 content pieces in week one — Atlas as chief of staff, Scout→Pitch→Quill→Vault→Ledger specialists, every chat owned by an outcome.
